title: The Two Rules of Resilience
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. offers a two-part rule for handling adversity that he teaches both his ninth graders and his own children. It began after a frustrating family episode in which a daughter hid under a stairwell rather than leave her aunt's home. Together with the kids he arrived at accepting what is happening and then making the best of it, drawing on Viktor Frankl's freedom to choose one's attitude. He kept the lessons alive by quizzing the children on the rules and praising them whenever they used them. He then extends the rules to teachers, who face disobedience, conflict, and frustrating work, and treats each setback as a chance to love, teach, and learn. The piece frames resilience as a main goal of high school, as important as academics.
points: Resilience can be reduced to two memorable rules: accept what is happening, then make the best of it.
Skills like this need repeated quizzing and specific praise when students show them.
Frankl's freedom of internal positioning supports the claim that attitude is always a choice.
The same rules apply to teachers dealing with disobedient students, conflict, and tedious work.
quotes: In Man’s Search for Meaning, Auschwitz survivor Viktor Frankl argues that there is a fundamental freedom that all people possess but too few exercise: the freedom of internal positioning. Frankl writes, “Everything can be taken away from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms—to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one’s own way.
I knew I needed to speak with my children about this pattern of responding negatively (and counter-productively) to circumstances we don’t like. Not knowing exactly what to say, I started talking.

Like always, the learning took time. In the hours and days that followed, I quizzed my daughters on the two rules quite a bit. I quizzed them until they could easily tell me what the two rules were. I quizzed them until their eyes started to flinch into a rolling motion as they said, “Accept what’s happening, Dad. Make the best of it.
And when I would see them responding differently to unwanted circumstances, I’d pull them aside and call it out. “Laura, I just saw you do that! You accepted what was happening. Nice.

The beautiful thing about these two rules of resilience is that they are as relevant to me (and to you!) as they are to my kids. When my kids are disobedient, or my wife and I are starting to argue, or work is a bummer, I’ll be best off if I 1) accept what’s happening and then 2) make the best of it.
